PROGRESS

elements.text:
A total of 63 applications had been accepted by 15
May 1989. The applications are for a range of plant
species and Australian and overseas applicants.

elements.text:

of the Journal and are listed in Part 2. They include
a schlumbergera, a rose and two grasses. It is
anticipated that several more rights will be granted
in July.

elements.text: PROPAGATION — apomictic species

lines.text: PROPAGATION — apomictic species

elements.text:
The amendment to the Act to give the grantee the
exclusive right to asexually propagate, or license
others to asexually propagate, a protected variety
for the commercial production of fruit, cut flowers
or other products is progressing.

lines.text: The amendment to the Act to give the grantee the
exclusive right to asexually propagate, or license
others to asexually propagate, a protected variety
for the commercial production of fruit, cut flowers
or other products is progressing.

elements.text:
The amendment will only apply to genera and
species prescribed for the purpose and the grantee
will be required to license anyone to asexually
propagate the variety if they meet reasonable
licence conditions.

lines.text: The amendment will only apply to genera and
species prescribed for the purpose and the grantee
will be required to license anyone to asexually
propagate the variety if they meet reasonable
licence conditions.

elements.text:
Comment was sought on genera and species which
should and should not be covered by the
amendment. No specific exclusions have been
sought and all genera and species will be covered
by the provision as they become eligible for PVR
unless there are specific reasons for their exclusion
(NOTE this amendment applies to asexual
propagation and does not include propagation
from seed).

lines.text: Comment was sought on genera and species which
should and should not be covered by the
amendment. No specific exclusions have been
sought and all genera and species will be covered
by the provision as they become eligible for PVR
unless there are specific reasons for their exclusion
(NOTE this amendment applies to asexual
propagation and does not include propagation
from seed).

elements.text:
Some consideration is being given to the need to
exclude apomictic species from the provisions of
the amendment. These are generally reproduced
from seed but without fertilisation (ie asexually). As
some grass species reproduce in this way
comment is sought (by 30 September 1989) on
whether or not such species should be excluded
from the provisions of the amendment.

elements.text:
COMPARATIVE GROWING TRIALS —
inclusion of varieties under
examination

lines.text: COMPARATIVE GROWING TRIALS —
inclusion of varieties under
examination

elements.text:
For a new variety to be eligible for PVR it must be
different from other known varieties. The PVR
Office requires applicants to demonstrate this
distinctness by growing the new variety with the
closest available varieties in comparative trials.

lines.text: For a new variety to be eligible for PVR it must be
different from other known varieties. The PVR
Office requires applicants to demonstrate this
distinctness by growing the new variety with the
closest available varieties in comparative trials.

elements.text:
Potential applicants should ensure that they are
aware of any new varieties currently under
examination by the PVR Office, as these may need
to be included in the comparative trials.

lines.text: Potential applicants should ensure that they are

elements.text:
Applicants should also note that they may be
required to give material of new varieties to other
applicants for comparative trials. In most cases
such material would be covered by provisional
protection.

elements.text:
COMPARATIVE TRIALS — Fruit
Varieties

lines.text: COMPARATIVE TRIALS — Fruit
Varieties

elements.text:
Some applicants have sought advice on methods
to reduce the long lead time for trials on fruit trees.
Experience has shown that this can be reduced
considerably by grafting the new varieties onto
mature rootstocks (in such cases all trial varieties
should be on the same age stocks) or onto mature
trees (several varieties can be grafted to the one
tree).

lines.text: Some applicants have sought advice on methods
to reduce the long lead time for trials on fruit trees.
Experience has shown that this can be reduced
considerably by grafting the new varieties onto
mature rootstocks (in such cases all trial varieties

trees (several varieties can be grafted to the one
tree).

elements.text:
If mature fruit characteristics are not of prime
importance, measurements may be taken at an
earlier stage. In addition laboratory assays can be
used to demonstrate differences, although some
field data will also be required.

should include in their trials comparisons with
similar varieties commonly available in Australia.

published if such comparative data is available.
Otherwise publication will be delayed until
Australian trials are complete.
